overview:
The Philistines carry the captured ark to Ashdod and set it beside the image of their god Dagon. Next morning Dagon lies on his face before the ark. They stand him up, and the following morning he is down again, his head and both hands broken off on the threshold. Then the LORD’s hand falls on Ashdod with tumors and death. The ark is moved to Gath, where tumors break out on small and great, and then to Ekron, whose people cry out as it arrives. The Philistine lords meet and agree to send it home.

The captured God fights alone. No Israelite appears in the chapter, and no prophet or priest explains anything; the Philistines name the cause themselves: “his hand is sore upon us, and upon Dagon our god” (v. 7).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it soon after the events (11th–10th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older court and prophetic sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Directly after the battle of chapter 4; the ark stays in Philistine country seven months (6:1).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Three of the five Philistine cities: Ashdod near the coast, with its temple of Dagon, and Gath and Ekron inland toward the hills.

hermeneutics:
Victors brought their enemies’ sacred objects home and set them before their own gods. Mesha, king of Moab, boasts on his stele (c. 840 BC) that he took the vessels of YHWH from Nebo and dragged them before his god Chemosh. Setting the ark “by Dagon” in Dagon’s house (v. 2) was the same act: a captured god displayed as tribute to the winner. The next two mornings turn the display around. Dagon lies face down “before the ark of the LORD,” the posture of a subject before his king, and the second time his head and hands lie broken off on the threshold.

Plague was a god’s hand. About 1350 BC the king of Alashiya (Cyprus) wrote to the pharaoh to explain a small shipment of copper: the hand of Nergal, his lord, had killed the men of his land, and not one copper-worker was left (Amarna letter EA 35). Nergal was the Mesopotamian god of plague and the dead. The Philistines use the same idiom: the hand of the LORD is heavy on them (vv. 6, 9, 11). They read their sickness the way their world did, as the act of an offended god, and their question is only which god and what he wants.

The text itself handles the disease delicately. In vv. 6, 9 and 12 the consonants written in the Hebrew spell *ofalim*, “swellings,” but the Masoretes marked them to be read aloud as *tehorim*; the Talmud lists this word among coarse terms that are read in a refined form (Megillah 25b, on Deuteronomy 28:27). The Septuagint also differs on the route: in v. 10 it sends the ark from Gath to Ascalon, not Ekron.

breakdown.label: The ark set beside Dagon in Ashdod
Dagon falls twice; the threshold custom
Tumors at Ashdod: “his hand is sore upon us”
The ark carried to Gath; tumors on small and great
Ekron cries out; the lords urge sending it back
The ark sent home on a new cart

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence through three Philistine cities, each worse than the last.

rows.text: Ashdod: Dagon falls; the hand is heavy
Ekron: a deadly destruction; the cry goes up

notes: **Dagon and the ark:** Dagon is named 11 times in vv. 2–7 and the ark 12 times in the chapter. After v. 7 Dagon is never named again; the ark goes on alone.

**Hands:** Dagon’s hands lie cut off on the threshold (v. 4), while the LORD’s hand (*yad*) acts in vv. 6, 7, 9 and 11. It is “heavy” (*kabed*) in vv. 6 and 11, the root of the glory that departed in 4:21–22.

**Rising alarm:** each city fares worse. Ashdod is destroyed and smitten (v. 6), Gath suffers “a very great destruction” (v. 9), and Ekron cries out as soon as the ark arrives (v. 10), until “the cry of the city went up to heaven” (v. 12).

Chapter 5 is the middle of the ark narrative (4:1–7:1). Chapter 4 ended with the glory gone from Israel; here it acts in exile, and 6:1 continues with seven months in Philistine country and the plan to send the ark back.

**Echoes:** the Philistines who recalled the plagues on Egypt (4:8) now suffer them. Psalm 78:66 sums up the episode: the LORD “smote his enemies in the hinder parts.” The LORD’s hand stays against the Philistines “all the days of Samuel” (7:13).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 9, where the LORD’s hand is against Gath, gathers Restoration passages on the hand of God against peoples. Moroni introduces the Jaredites as a people destroyed by the hand of the Lord, and the revelation on war of December 1832 warns that plague, famine and earthquake will make the nations feel “the chastening hand of an Almighty God.” Mormon 5:23 asks readers whether they know they are in the hands of God.
traditions.cite: 1 Samuel 5:9, footnote a; Ether 1:1; D&C 87:6; Mormon 5:23

traditions.text: Rabbi Yohanan and Resh Lakish disagree about why the Philistines set the ark beside Dagon (v. 2). Rabbi Yohanan says they meant to honour it, reasoning that one god should dwell beside another. Resh Lakish says they meant the reverse: this one conquered and that one was conquered, so let the conquered serve the conqueror. His reading is the victor’s custom seen on the Mesha stele (see Hermeneutics).

The same two rabbis argue whether a broken idol stays forbidden. Rabbi Yohanan cites vv. 4–5: Dagon was broken, yet his priests still honoured the threshold, so worshipers do not give up a broken god. Resh Lakish answers that they abandoned Dagon and began to worship the threshold instead, saying Dagon’s spirit had left the image and rested there.

Josephus says the Philistines put the ark beside Dagon “as one of their spoils,” and in the morning found Dagon paying it worship, lying prostrate in adoration. The disease at Ashdod is a sudden, fatal dysentery, and mice rise from the ground to ruin the crops. Like the Septuagint he sends the ark to Ascalon, and has it go round all five cities.

The Philistines bring the ark into Dagon’s temple to ask Dagon about their next campaign and find him fallen, his hands and feet laid before the ark. They crucify his priests, and on the second morning find the same. God had promised Samuel that the Philistines would perish by scorpions and creeping things, and at Ekron the creeping things destroy pregnant women, nursing mothers and infants.

The midrash ties this chapter to the Philistines’ boast in 4:8. Their wicked had said Israel’s God spent his plagues on Egypt and had none left, so God answers with a plague never seen before: a mouse comes up from the deep as a man sits at his needs and drags out his bowels. When they turn to seats, the mouse tells the seat it is the messenger of the One who spoke and the world came to be, and the seat splits.

On v. 5 Kimhi cites a midrash of Rabbi Jeremiah: Israel was more zealous in idolatry than the nations. Of the Philistines it is written that they would not tread on Dagon’s threshold, but of Israel the prophet says, “I will punish all those that leap on the threshold” (Zephaniah 1:9). The Philistine custom becomes a rebuke to Israel.

Kimhi reports a tradition that Dagon was shaped like a fish from the navel down and like a man above, which is why he was called Dagon (from *dag*, “fish”). On that reading “only the stump of Dagon” left in v. 4 means only the fish-part remained once the head and hands broke off. Modern scholars derive the name from a Semitic word for grain instead.

Rashi explains the *tehorim* of v. 6 as a disease of the rectum and adds that mice entered the bowels of the people of Ashdod and dragged out their entrails. On v. 9 he notes a Masoretic spelling: the verb “had emerods” is written with one letter and read as another, giving “they were struck in their hidden parts.” His mice match those of Josephus and Sulpicius Severus and the golden mice sent back with the ark (6:4–5).

In his short sacred history the Gallic writer says the image “dedicated to a demon” fell when the ark was brought in and was torn to pieces the next night when set up again. He then has mice spring up across the country and kill many thousands with venomous bites, so that the men of Ashdod move the ark to escape. Like Josephus and the Septuagint, he sends it on from Gath to Ascalon, where the chief men of the nation decide to return it to the Hebrews.

CLASH CHECK (Nov 2026): judges-016 and judges-010 use Dagon’s Syrian background (Dagan at Mari, Ebla, Emar, Ugarit; fish etymology rejected), so Hermeneutics here uses no Dagon background; Radak’s fish tradition appears only in Traditions as an old reading, with the modern grain derivation in one clause. 1-samuel-006 uses the LXX mice of 5:6, the swellings/bubonic plague link, Apollo Smintheus, Avodah Zarah 24b, and Josephus 6.1.2–4; this chapter avoids the mice as a Hermeneutics point and uses Josephus 6.1.1 and Avodah Zarah 41b. The Mesha stele is used widely (deuteronomy-002, genesis-022, judges-011 and others) for land claims, herem and child sacrifice; the YHWH vessels before Chemosh are not used elsewhere. joshua-013 uses the Ekron inscription; not used here.
